explain.say: Add odd numbers: 1 is 1, 1 plus 3 is 4, plus 5 is 9, plus 7 is 16. All squares! Is that true forever? You cannot check every number. Look at the first stage: the claim that the first n odd numbers add to n squared.

stages.label: Base case: n = 1
stages.ask: What is the base case in induction?

stages.label: All dominoes fall
stages.note: True for every whole number n.
stages.ask: Why does induction prove it for every number?

explain.say: Think of an endless row of dominoes. First, knock over domino 1. Check n equals 1: the sum is just 1, and 1 squared is 1. True! See the second stage? This is the base case.

stages.label: Base case: n = 1
stages.ask: What is the base case in induction?

stages.label: All dominoes fall
stages.note: True for every whole number n.
stages.ask: Why does induction prove it for every number?

explain.say: Next, imagine domino k has fallen: suppose the first k odd numbers add to k squared. Look at the third stage. We do not know which k, it could be any. Now, does domino k plus 1 fall too?

stages.label: Base case: n = 1
stages.ask: What is the base case in induction?

stages.label: All dominoes fall
stages.note: True for every whole number n.
stages.ask: Why does induction prove it for every number?

explain.say: The next odd number is 2k plus 1. Add it: k squared plus 2k plus 1, which is k plus 1, all squared. Yes! Look at the fourth stage. If any domino falls, the next one falls too. This is the inductive step.

stages.label: Base case: n = 1
stages.ask: What is the base case in induction?

stages.label: All dominoes fall
stages.note: True for every whole number n.
stages.ask: Why does induction prove it for every number?

explain.say: The first domino falls, and each one knocks the next, so they all fall. Look at the last stage: true for every n. Brilliant! Mathematicians use induction to prove facts about infinitely many numbers with just two steps.

faq.q: How does proof by induction work?
faq.a: Show the statement is true for the first case, the base case. Then show that if it is true for any k, it is true for k plus 1. Together these prove it for every whole number.

faq.q: What is the base case in induction?
faq.a: The first case you check directly, usually n equals 1. It is like knocking over the first domino.
asks: Why do we need a base case?

faq.a: The part where you assume the statement is true for some k and prove it must then be true for k plus 1. It shows each domino knocks over the next.
asks: How do you do the inductive step?

faq.q: Why does induction prove it for every number?
faq.a: Case 1 is true. Then the step makes case 2 true, which makes case 3 true, and so on forever. No whole number is missed.

faq.q: Why is the sum of the first n odd numbers n squared?
faq.a: Picture an n by n square of dots. Each new odd number adds an L-shaped layer around it, making the next square. Induction turns that picture into a proof.
asks: Why do odd numbers add up to squares?

facts: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n²: 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1) = n².
A proof by induction needs a base case and an inductive step from k to k + 1.
